div.p: The task set in some real-time systems consists of adaptive variable-rate (AVR) tasks and time-triggered tasks. AVR tasks generate instances when the rotating source rotates to some special angles. Time-triggered tasks generate jobs irregularly under the constraint of minimum release time interval. Response time analysis (RTA) is an effective method to test the schedulability of tasks. The consideration on angular phase is conducive to improve the accuracy of RTAs. To the best of our knowledge, there is only one RTA method that considers angular phases and supports hybrid tasks. However, this method is incorrect since it may misjudge some unschedulable task sets as schedulable task sets. In this work, we propose the first correct RTA method that considers angular phases. The theoretical analysis proves the correctness of our method.
Index Terms-Response time analysis, hybrid tasks, AVR tasks, FP scheduling, angular phase.
108 2022 IEEE 28th Real-Time and Embedded Technology and Applications Symposium (RTAS)

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The real-time system has been widely used in many fields. Tasks in real-time systems can be divided into adaptive variable-rate (AVR) tasks and time-triggered tasks. AVR tasks generate instances when the rotating source rotates to some special angles. Time-triggered tasks generate jobs irregularly under the constraint of minimum release time interval. AVR tasks and time-triggered tasks may exist in a system at the same time. For example, a vehicle control system conducts fuel injection once the engine crankshaft rotates to some specific angles (by executing an AVR task). At the same time, it accesses the CAN bus every 50 milliseconds to obtain the current speed (by executing a time-triggered task).

Time-triggered tasks have deadlines. AVR tasks have deadline angles. The real-time system needs to guarantee that all time-triggered tasks it executed can finish their execution before their deadlines, and all AVR tasks it executed can finish their execution before the rotating source rotates to their deadline angles. So, the real-time system will execute a schedulability analysis method (to judge the schedulability of tasks) once the currently executed task set changes.

Response time analysis (RTA) is a typical schedulability analysis method, calculates the worst-case response time (WCRT) of each time-triggered task and the worst-case response angle (WCRA) of each AVR task. However, most of the existing RTAs either assume that all AVR tasks have a common angular period or that all AVR tasks generate instances at the same time. The rest of the existing RTAs have the problem of low calculation accuracy. The consideration on angular phase is conducive to improve the accuracy of RTAs. RTA-FS, named according to authors' names, is the only RTA that considers angular phases and supports hybrid tasks [1]. But, it will misjudge some unschedulable task sets as schedulable task sets. So, it is necessary to design a correct and accurate RTA method for hybrid tasks.
We study the RTA method for hybrid tasks under fixed priority (FP) scheduling. The main contributions are as follows.
• The reason why RTA-FS may misjudge unschedulable task sets as schedulable task sets is analyzed.
• A new RTA method is proposed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first correct RTA method that considers angular phases and supports hybrid tasks.

• The theoretical analysis proves the correctness of the proposed method. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the existing schedulability analysis for hybrid task sets. Section III presents the system model. Section IV analyzes the state-of-the-art RTA for hybrid tasks under FP scheduling. Section V introduces a new RTA method. Section VI evaluates the performance of the proposed method in term of acceptance ratio. Section VII draws a conclusion. II. RELATED WORK Kim et al. proposed the first schedulability analysis for task sets containing only one AVR task with the highest priority [2]. Pollex et al. simplified the relation between task execution time and task release environment, and led to two pessimistic analysis methods [3], [4]. Buttle proposed a classical AVR task model [5], which is used by most later scholars [6]- [8]. Davis et al. found the maximum interference by considering a combination of the task parameters and using integer linear programming, but they need to quantify the angular velocity [9]. Biondi et al. proposed the concept of dominant velocity to calculate the worst-case interference from the AVR task by finding a finite set of cases in the velocity domain [10]. Based on this approach, [11] derived an exact response time analysis, [12] extended to arbitrary but bounded accelerations, and proposed an additional pruning rule that reduces the running time, [13] calculated demand bound function (DBF) under EDF scheduling. Bijinemula et al. used the Knapsack-Based approach to calculate DBF under EDF scheduling [14]. In addition to these RTAs, [15]- [18] proposed utilizationbased schedulability analysis methods. Besides, there are also some studies [19], [20] that convert AVR tasks into Digraph Real-Time (DRT) tasks, so that existing schedulability analysis methods for DRT tasks can be used. See details in recent survey papers [21], [22].

All above studies ignore the phase constraints between the release angles of AVR tasks. Feld and Slomka improved the method proposed in [23] by calculating task execution mode based on the angular phases [1].

div.head: A. Model and Assumptions
div.p: We consider a task set Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n } scheduled under a traditional FP scheduling, rate monotonic (RM) scheduling, in a uniprocessor system, where n is the number of tasks and τ i is the i-th task in Γ. Each task τ i is either an AVR task or a time-triggered task. We denote a task τ i by τ a i if it is an AVR task. Otherwise, we denote it by τ t i . We use Γ a i to represent the task set consisting of all AVR tasks with higher priorities than τ i , and use Γ t i to represent the task set consisting of all time-triggered tasks with higher priorities than τ i .

Rotating source and event are two important concepts. The state of the rotating source can be characterized by a 3-tuple: (θ, ω, α), where θ is the angular position, ω ∈ [ω min , ω max ] is the angular velocity, and α ∈ [α min , α max ] is the angular acceleration (α min < 0 < α max ). Events refer to the arrivals of the rotating source at some specific angles (in relation to the beginning angle of current angular work cycle). The angular work cycle is the longest angular distance after which the pattern of events repeats itself. We use ζ to represent the length of the angular work cycle. For example, given an angular work cycle with length 360°and an event corresponding to angle 60°, we can get that this event occurs once the rotating source rotates to x • 360°+ 60°, where x is a non-negative integer.

Each AVR task τ a i corresponds to an event set E i = {e i,1 , e i,2 , ..., e i,ni }, where e i,j is the j-th event of τ a i . Each event e i,j has a relative release angle r a i,j and a relative deadline angle D i,j (D i,j ≤ ζ). Once the rotating source rotates to y satisfying (yr a i,j ) mod ζ = 0, τ a i will generate an instance ϕ i,j that should be completed before the rotating source reaches y + D i,j . ϕ i,j is generated in each angular work cycle. We use Φ i,j to represent the instance set consisting of all ϕ i,j s. For each AVR task τ a i with an event set E i = {e i,1 , e i,2 , ..., e i,ni }, we use Φ i = {ϕ i,1 , ϕ i,2 , ..., ϕ i,ni } to represent the AVR instance set of τ a i in any angular work cycle. Each AVR task τ a i has multiple execution modes. We use M i to represent the number of the execution modes of τ a i . Because each execution mode corresponds to a different piece of code, each execution mode corresponds to a different worst-case execution time (WCET). Because the execution mode adopted by an AVR instance ϕ i,j (of τ a i ) depends on the instantaneous angular velocity when ϕ i,j is released, the WCET of ϕ i,j depends on the instantaneous angular velocity when it is released. For each AVR task τ a i , the angular velocity range [ω min , ω max ] can be divided into M i subranges corresponding to the M i execution modes. We use Ω i,j = (ω - i,j , ω + i,j ] to represent the j-th sub-range and use C i (ω) to represent the WCET whose corresponding sub-range contains ω. In addition, each instance ϕ i,j has a response time and a response angle. The response time is the time gap between the release time and the execution finish time. The response angle is the angular distance between the release angle and the execution finish angle. The upper bound of the response time of ϕ i,j is the worst-case response time (WCRT) of ϕ i,j . The upper bound of the response angle of ϕ i,j is the worst-case response angle (WCRA) of ϕ i,j . The instantaneous angular velocity when ϕ i,j is released has a direct impact on the WCRT and WCRA of ϕ i,j . We use R i,j (ω) to represent the WCRT of ϕ i,j under the condition that the instantaneous angular velocity is equal to ω, and use A i,j (ω) to represent the WCRA of ϕ i,j under the same condition. Moreover, we use R i,j to represent the WCRT of ϕ i,j under any angular velocity, and use A i,j to represent the WCRA of ϕ i,j (under any angular velocity). R i,j is also called the WCRT of e i,j . A i,j is also called the WCRA of e i,j . An AVR instance ϕ i,j is schedulable if
div.formula: A i,j ≤ D i,j . An AVR task τ i is schedulable if A i,j ≤ D i,j for each ϕ i,j .
div.p: Each time-triggered task τ t i can be characterized by a 3tuple: (C i , D i , T i ), where C i is the WCET, D i is the relative deadline and T i (D i ≤ T i ) is the minimum inter-arrival time (also called period for brevity). Each task τ t i can generate an infinite or finite stream of jobs that inherit the parameters of τ t i . We use J i,j to denote the j-th job generated by τ t i . Each job J i,j has a release time r i,j , an execution finish time f i,j and an absolute deadline d i,j = r i,j + D i . The response time of a job J i,j is the time gap between its release time and its execution finish time. Since the angular velocity of the rotating source affects the response time of J i,j , we use R i,j (ω) to represent the upper bound of the response time of J i,j under the condition that the instantaneous angular velocity at r i,j is equal to ω. R i,j (ω) is also called the WCRT of J i,j under ω. In addition, we use R i (ω) to represent the largest R i,j (ω), j ≥ 1, and use R i to represent the largest R i (ω), ω ∈ [ω min , ω max ]. We call R i (ω) the WCRT of τ t i under ω, and call R i the WCRT of τ t i . Table I shows the notations used in this paper.
The following assumptions are made:
• All AVR tasks share a common rotating source.
• The angular acceleration may change at any time.
• The priority of τ i is higher than τ j iff i < j.
• r i,j+1r i,j ≥ T i for each two jobs J i,j and J i,j+1 .

div.head: B. Interference
div.p: Given an instance ϕ i,j (or a job J i,j ), the interference time on ϕ i,j (or J i,j ) is the cumulative time in which ϕ i,j (or J i,j ) has been released but can not be executed due to the execution of higher priority tasks. The interference angle on ϕ i,j (or J i,j ) is the cumulative angle through which the rotating source rotates during the time in which ϕ i,j (or J i,j ) has been released but can not be executed due to the execution of higher priority tasks. "Interference time" is also used to represent the upper bound of the interference time. "Interference angle" is also used to represent the upper bound of the interference angle.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: Using "OUR" to represent the RTA method proposed in this paper and using "PFS" to represent the method proposed in [3], we compare the performances of "OUR", "PFS" and "RTA-FS" in term of acceptance ratio. Acceptance ratio refers to the proportion of schedulable task sets in all test task sets.

div.head: A. Parameter Setting
div.p: In our experiments, we follow a similar method as in [3] and [1] to generate task sets. The data on a practical auto engine is used in our experiments [3].

System parameters. We considered a system with 5 timetriggered tasks and 5 AVR tasks. All AVR tasks share a common rotating source and the length of the angular work cycle is equal to 2160°= 6×360°. The angular velocity of the rotating source is limited in [1000rpm, 5000rpm]. We quantized the velocity range into 100 subranges Ω m s as in [1]. The angular acceleration is limited in [-100r/s 2 , 100r/s 2 ]. The Rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling is used to schedule these 10 tasks. For each AVR task τ a i , min ∀ϕi,j ∈Φi (r a i,j+1 -r a i,j )/ω max is taken as its period. The default total utilization of these 10 tasks, U , is equal to 0.85. The default proportion of the total utilization of AVR tasks in U , ρ u , satisfies the uniform distribution in (0, 1). The UUnifast-discard method [26] is used to generate the utilization of each task.

Parameters of time-triggered tasks. For each timetriggered task τ t i , the period T i satisfies the log-uniform distribution in [10ms, 100ms], the deadline D i satisfies the uniform distribution in [C i + 0.25(T i -C i ), T i ], where the WCET C i is obtained by

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: Figure 3 shows the experimental result. It can be get that:

• The acceptance ratios of both "OUR" and "PFS" can reach 100% when U < 0.4. "OUR" has a better performance than "PFS" in term of acceptance ratio when U ≥ 0.4. • The acceptance ratios of both "OUR" and "PFS" decrease with the growth of U , and increase with the growth of M i , Ev i and ρ u . • The absolute improvement ratio of "OUR" on "PFS" is about 10% on average.

• The acceptance ratio of "RTA-FS" sometimes is higher than "OUR" since some unschedulable task sets will be misjudged as "schedulable" under "RTA-FS". The acceptance ratio of "OUR" sometimes is higher than "RTA-FS" since "OUR" has a higher accuracy than "RTA-FS".

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: An existing RTA method for hybrid tasks under FP scheduling is reviewed and the reason why it will misjudge some unschedulable task sets as "schedulable" is pointed out. A new RTA method is proposed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first correct RTA method that considers angular phases and supports hybrid tasks under FP scheduling. The theoretical analysis proves the correctness of this method. Experimental results verify the performance of this method.
